segments.t: Chef Barinov is woken up in Elena Pavlovna's bedroom by an early morning call from Lyova, who says he and his mother are worried because Barinov never came home. Embarrassed to tell the truth, the Chef claims he spent the night at the restaurant.
Right, let's take their exchange slowly and unpack the Russian.
'Have a conscience, let me sleep.' Barinov counters right away beside Lyova, steering the talk right where he wants it.
'Lyova, what do you want?' Barinov centers one classic piece in reply: "nado" means "it is necessary", and it carries the main weight of what Barinov is saying.
'You did not come home last night.' Barinov gives the reaction with ease: spoken Russian trims this down to just 4 words, dropping the extra helper words that English has to spell out.
'Mom and I are worried about you.' Lyova fires back calmly with Barinov, letting the remark speak for itself.
'Where are you?' Barinov sends the thought with warmth: notice how Russian needs no word for "am", "is", or "are" in the present — placing the words side by side says it all.
'I spent the night at the restaurant.' Lyova delivers this update without pause: spoken Russian trims this down to just 4 words, dropping the extra helper words that English has to spell out.
'Right now I just stepped out briefly to the...' Barinov speaks evenly across the room, to clear the air between them once and for all.
'And what are you doing over there?' Lyova chooses one sharp expression in earnest: "delayete" means "are doing" (from "delat"), giving the line its exact edge.

'What business am I tending to?' Barinov voices the remark without fuss: Russian keeps the exact word order of a normal statement here, turning it into a question for Lyova purely through rising pitch at the end.
'I will be back soon.' Lyova cuts in firmly with a nod, without trying to dress up how he really feels.
'You are acting like a child.' Barinov focuses on one pointed piece at once: "rebenok" means "child", and it carries the main weight of what Barinov is saying.
'Come on, Lyova is a grown man.' Barinov hands over the thought without pause: notice how Russian needs no word for "am", "is", or "are" in the present — placing the words side by side says it all.
'You could have just told him the truth.' Barinov reacts pointedly as they talk, before Lyova can change the subject.
That wraps up this scene as waking up in Elena Pavlovna's bed, Chef Barinov answers a worried morning phone call from Lyova and lies that he slept at the restaurant. Until next time!
